title: Prompt Caching, Streaming, Quotas & Cost per Request
scopeHtml: Scope: Reusing processed prompt context, SSE streaming, provider quotas and token-based cost per request.

notes.title: Why caching, streaming, quotas and cost belong together
notes.html:
Four ideas decide whether an LLM feature is pleasant, affordable and reliable. We take them one by one, but they interlock, so first the vocabulary.

  • Token: the chunk of text a model reads and writes (roughly 3 to 4 English characters, about three quarters of a word). Providers bill and rate-limit in tokens, not in characters or requests.
  • Prompt: everything you send in one request: system instructions, tool definitions, documents, chat history, and the new user message.
  • Input tokens / output tokens: what you send versus what the model generates. Output is usually priced several times higher than input (verify current price pages).
  • Prompt caching: the provider remembers the already-processed beginning of your prompt, so the next request that starts with the same text is cheaper and faster.
  • Streaming: the server sends the answer piece by piece as it is generated instead of waiting for the whole thing. The wire format is usually SSE (Server-Sent Events).
  • Quota / rate limit: the ceiling a provider puts on how many requests and tokens you may use per minute (and sometimes per day or per month in money).
  • Cost per request: the arithmetic tokens x price for one call, and the multiplication that turns it into a monthly bill.

How they connect:

 user message
     |
     v
 [your backend] --(1) estimate tokens, check your own budget/quota
     |
     |--(2) build prompt: STATIC part first (cacheable), DYNAMIC part last
     v
 [provider API] -- cache hit?  yes: cheap + fast prefill
     |                         no : full price, write cache
     |--(3) stream tokens back as SSE events  ---> user sees text after ~0.5 s
     |--(4) final usage block: input / cache_read / cache_write / output tokens
     v
 [your backend] --(5) cost = sum(tokens x price), log it, update quota counters

Why it exists: a model is a metered, rate-limited, slow-to-first-answer service. Caching attacks the repeated bill and the latency of re-reading the same context. Streaming attacks perceived latency. Quotas protect the provider (and your wallet) from overload. Cost calculation is how you notice that one of the other three is broken.

See also (existing notes): C2 01_I1 covers streaming and perceived latency from the serving side, 02_Q1 covers caching layers (response and semantic caches), and 03_C1 covers token economics and budgets in general. These notes go deeper on the API-side mechanism: how provider prompt caching really works, the SSE wire format and its failure modes, quota algorithms with code, and exact per-request cost maths.

Real life. A restaurant: caching is keeping the stock simmering instead of boiling it from scratch per order, streaming is bringing dishes as they are ready, quotas are the number of tables, and cost per request is the itemized receipt.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "caching" without saying which cache. Provider prompt caching, your own response cache and a semantic cache are three different things with different correctness risks.
  • Forgetting that output tokens, not only input tokens, are billed and often dominate the price of chatty answers.
  • Treating requests per minute as the only limit; token limits usually bind first.

notes.title: Prompt caching: what it is and why it exists
notes.html:
Plain words. When you send a prompt, the model first runs a prefill phase: it reads every input token and builds an internal memory of them called the KV cache (keys and values of the attention layers; see 01_I1 for the mechanism). Prefill is real GPU work and grows with prompt length. If the next request starts with exactly the same 20,000 tokens (same system prompt, same document), redoing that prefill is waste. Prompt caching lets the provider keep that processed prefix for a short time and reuse it. You pay a reduced price for the reused part and the first token arrives sooner.

Why it exists. Real prompts are mostly static. A coding assistant resends tool definitions plus a repo summary on every turn. A support bot resends a 6,000-token policy document with every question. A chat resends the whole history each turn. Without caching you pay full price for the same bytes again and again.

What it is NOT.

  • It does not cache the answer. The model still generates a fresh output each time; only the input processing is reused. So the answer can still differ and temperature still applies.
  • It is not a semantic cache. A single changed character early in the prompt means a miss for everything after it.
  • It does not change output quality; the model sees exactly the same tokens either way.

Who offers what (fast-moving, verify against the docs):

Provider How it is turned on What you see
Anthropic You mark blocks with cache_control (explicit breakpoints); there is also an automatic mode in newer API versions (verify) usage.cache_creation_input_tokens, usage.cache_read_input_tokens
OpenAI Automatic for prompts above a minimum length (about 1,024 tokens, verify) usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens
Google Gemini Implicit caching plus explicit cached-content objects with a TTL (verify) usage_metadata.cached_content_token_count
Self-hosted vLLM / SGLang Automatic prefix caching (APC / RadixAttention) server metrics for prefix hit rate

The self-hosted variant is the same idea at the GPU level: vLLM keeps KV blocks of finished requests and reuses them if a new request shares the prefix (see PagedAttention in 01_I1).

Real life. A teacher who has already read the 30-page case study aloud to the class. New questions about it start from "we all know the story" instead of rereading all 30 pages.

Common interview traps.

  • "Prompt caching makes responses deterministic." No; it caches input processing only.
  • "Caching works on similar prompts." It works only on an exact prefix match, token for token.
  • Confusing prompt caching (provider side, prefix reuse) with an application-level response cache.

notes.title: How provider prompt caching works step by step
notes.html:
Take Anthropic's explicit model as the worked example, since it makes the mechanics visible. (Details such as minimum lengths and TTLs are fast-moving: verify in the docs.)

  1. The request is built in a fixed order: tools, then system, then messages. Caching is on this prefix order.
  2. You place a cache breakpoint ("cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}) on the last block you want included in the cached prefix.
  3. The provider hashes the whole prefix up to that breakpoint. If a stored entry with the same hash exists and is still alive, it is a cache read (hit). If not, the provider processes the prefix normally and stores it: a cache write (creation).
  4. A write costs a premium over normal input (commonly 1.25x for the default short TTL, around 2x for the longer 1-hour option; verify). A read costs a small fraction (commonly about 0.1x, verify).
  5. Each hit refreshes the entry's lifetime. Default TTL is a few minutes (5 minutes, verify); an idle prefix expires.
  6. There is a minimum cacheable length (on the order of 1,024 tokens for bigger models and 2,048 for the smallest; verify). Shorter prefixes are silently not cached: no error, you just see zeros in the usage fields.
  7. The response tells you what happened in the usage block.
 Request 1:  [tools][system][doc 18,000 tok]*  [user: Q1]
                                   ^ breakpoint
   -> cache MISS: cache_creation_input_tokens = 18,000 (write, 1.25x)
 Request 2 (within TTL):
             [tools][system][doc 18,000 tok]*  [user: Q2]
   -> cache HIT : cache_read_input_tokens = 18,000 (read, 0.1x), input_tokens = Q2 only
 Request 3 (doc edited by one word):
             [tools][system][doc' ...]*        [user: Q3]
   -> MISS again, full write. Everything before the edit could still hit,
      everything from the edit onward cannot.

Multi-turn chats. Put a breakpoint on the last message of the previous turn. Each new turn reads the whole earlier conversation from cache and writes only the new tail. The system looks backward from the breakpoint for earlier entries, so a moving breakpoint still hits the older prefix (verify the exact lookback rules; there is a documented limit on how far it searches and a cap on the number of breakpoints, currently four).

The break-even maths (shown). Let the cacheable prefix be P tokens, normal input price p, write multiplier 1.25, read multiplier 0.1, and n requests inside the TTL.

  • Without caching: n x P x p.
  • With caching: 1.25 x P x p + (n - 1) x 0.1 x P x p.
  • n = 1: 1.25 vs 1. A loss of 25% on that prefix.
  • n = 2: 1.25 + 0.1 = 1.35 vs 2. A saving of 32.5%.
  • n = 10: 1.25 + 0.9 = 2.15 vs 10. A saving of 78.5%.
  • So caching pays off from the second request inside the TTL. A prefix used once is a small loss.

Real life. A library photocopy service: the first copy of a long document costs extra set-up, every further copy within the day is nearly free, but if nobody asks again before closing time you wasted the set-up.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing cache writes are free. Writes cost more than normal input; one-off prompts should not be marked.
  • Putting the breakpoint after dynamic content. Then the prefix hash changes every call and you pay for a write every time.
  • Not knowing the order tools, then system, then messages. Editing a tool definition invalidates everything after it.

notes.title: Prompt caching in code
notes.html:
The pattern is always: static first with a breakpoint, dynamic last. Then read the usage fields to prove it works.

# pip install anthropic ; ANTHROPIC_API_KEY comes from the environment
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
POLICY = open("policy.txt").read()  # ~6,000 tokens, identical on every call

def ask(question: str):
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5",  # verify model id
        max_tokens=400,
        system=[
            {"type": "text", "text": "You are a support agent. Answer only from the policy."},
            {"type": "text", "text": POLICY,
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},   # breakpoint: cache everything up to here
        ],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],  # dynamic part, after the breakpoint
    )
    u = resp.usage
    # first call: cache_creation_input_tokens ~6000, cache_read_input_tokens 0
    # next call : cache_creation_input_tokens 0,     cache_read_input_tokens ~6000
    print(u.input_tokens, u.cache_creation_input_tokens, u.cache_read_input_tokens, u.output_tokens)
    return resp.content[0].text
// Kotlin: plain OkHttp REST so no SDK method names are assumed. Same JSON body as Python.
import okhttp3.*
import okhttp3.MediaType.Companion.toMediaType
import okhttp3.RequestBody.Companion.toRequestBody
import org.json.JSONArray
import org.json.JSONObject

val http = OkHttpClient()

fun ask(policy: String, question: String): JSONObject {
    val system = JSONArray()
        .put(JSONObject().put("type", "text").put("text", "Answer only from the policy."))
        .put(JSONObject().put("type", "text").put("text", policy)
            .put("cache_control", JSONObject().put("type", "ephemeral"))) // breakpoint
    val body = JSONObject()
        .put("model", "claude-sonnet-5-5") // verify model id
        .put("max_tokens", 400)
        .put("system", system)
        .put("messages", JSONArray().put(JSONObject().put("role", "user").put("content", question)))
    val req = Request.Builder()
        .url("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages")
        .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
        .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01")
        .post(body.toString().toRequestBody("application/json".toMediaType()))
        .build()
    http.newCall(req).execute().use { r ->
        val json = JSONObject(r.body!!.string())
        // json.usage has cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens
        println(json.getJSONObject("usage"))
        return json
    }
}
// Never put the API key in an Android app: call YOUR backend, which runs this code.
// Java 17: java.net.http, same JSON. (The anthropic-java SDK exposes the same fields;
// verify the exact builder method names in the SDK docs before relying on them.)
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;

public class CachedAsk {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String policy = java.nio.file.Files.readString(java.nio.file.Path.of("policy.txt"))
                .replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("\"", "\\\"").replace("\n", "\\n");
        String body = """
            {"model":"claude-sonnet-5-5","max_tokens":400,
             "system":[
               {"type":"text","text":"Answer only from the policy."},
               {"type":"text","text":"%s","cache_control":{"type":"ephemeral"}}],
             "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is the refund window?"}]}
            """.formatted(policy);
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"))
                .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
                .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01")
                .header("content-type", "application/json")
                .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        HttpResponse<String> res = HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        System.out.println(res.body()); // look for "cache_read_input_tokens" in the usage block
    }
}

OpenAI-style note. There is no code to add: caching is automatic for long enough prompts, and you only verify usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens > 0. The practical work is identical: keep the prefix stable and put variable text last.

Real products. Claude Code and similar coding agents rely heavily on caching of the system prompt, tool definitions and conversation prefix so that a 100-turn session does not re-bill the entire history each turn. Document-QA products cache the document once and ask many questions.

Real life. Labeling the "frequently used" shelf in a pantry. You arrange the shelf once, and everyone reaches for it quickly after that.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "I enabled caching" without checking cache_read_input_tokens. If it stays 0, you are paying the write premium or nothing is cached.
  • Putting a timestamp, request id or user name at the top of the system prompt. It breaks the hash on every request.
  • Forgetting that the Android client must not hold the key; caching is a backend concern.

notes.title: Prompt caching failure patterns in production
notes.html:
Most "caching does not work" tickets come from a short list. Learn them as a checklist.

  1. Volatile text in the prefix. A Current time: 14:03:22 line or a random request id at the top. Fix: move it to the end, or truncate to the day if the model needs a date.
  2. Non-deterministic serialization. JSON of tool definitions built from a hash map whose key order changes between processes, or pretty-printing differences between services. Two byte-different prompts hash differently. Fix: build the static prefix once, with sorted keys, and reuse the same object.
  3. Below the minimum length. A 700-token system prompt will never cache. The fix is not padding; it is accepting the full price (small anyway) or batching more static context.
  4. TTL expiry. Traffic of one request every 10 minutes with a 5-minute TTL means every call is a write at 1.25x, which is more expensive than no caching. Options: the longer TTL option, or a cheap "keep-warm" ping if the maths says so (and it only does when requests are frequent enough), or do not cache that prefix.
  5. Breakpoint count and placement. Too few breakpoints in a growing conversation means the cache never advances. Too many wastes the limited slots.
  6. Parameters that invalidate the cache. Changing tool definitions, tool choice settings, images, or some thinking settings mid-conversation can invalidate earlier prefixes (verify the invalidation table in the docs).
  7. Parallel cold start. 50 requests fire simultaneously on a cold prefix. None sees an existing entry, so all 50 pay the write. Fix: send one request first, wait for the first response (the entry becomes readable once the first response begins), then fan out.
  8. Cache is per organization/workspace and per model. Switching the model (Sonnet to Haiku) starts from zero; two different API keys in different workspaces do not share entries (verify isolation rules).
  9. Privacy. Cached prefixes are isolated to your account, but if your prefix includes one user's data, do not reuse it for another user: that is your application's bug, not the provider's.

Measuring. Track cache hit ratio as cache_read / (cache_read + cache_creation + input_tokens) per feature and alert when it falls. A sudden drop after a deploy usually means someone touched the prefix.

 healthy   : read 18,000 | write 0      | fresh 300   -> ratio 98%
 broken A  : read 0      | write 18,000 | fresh 300   -> prefix changes each call (volatile text)
 broken B  : read 0      | write 0      | fresh 18,300-> below minimum or caching never enabled

Real life. A bus that only waits at the stop for five minutes. If you arrive every ten minutes, you always find an empty stop and a bus that has to start from scratch.

Common interview traps.

  • "Our hit rate is 0, so the provider is broken." It is nearly always a changing prefix.
  • Warming the cache with N parallel requests; they all miss.
  • Assuming longer TTL is always better; the longer-TTL write costs more.

notes.title: SSE: what streaming responses are
notes.html:
The problem. A model generates roughly 30 to 100 tokens per second (very model dependent). A 600-token answer takes 6 to 20 seconds. If you wait for the complete response, the user stares at a spinner. Streaming sends each fragment as soon as it exists, so the first words appear in well under a second.

Why SSE. The browser and the HTTP world already have a standard for "server pushes a stream of text events over one HTTP response": Server-Sent Events. The server answers with Content-Type: text/event-stream and keeps the connection open, writing events. Compared with WebSockets: SSE is one-way (server to client), plain HTTP (works with load balancers, auth headers, retries), simple to implement, and ideal for token streams. WebSockets are for two-way realtime such as voice.

Wire format. Each event is a few lines field: value, ended by a blank line. The fields are event:, data:, optional id: and retry:. A line starting with : is a comment, often used as a keep-alive.

event: message_start
data: {"type":"message_start","message":{"id":"msg_01...","role":"assistant","usage":{"input_tokens":412,"output_tokens":1}}}

event: content_block_start
data: {"type":"content_block_start","index":0,"content_block":{"type":"text","text":""}}

event: content_block_delta
data: {"type":"content_block_delta","index":0,"delta":{"type":"text_delta","text":"Hel"}}

event: content_block_delta
data: {"type":"content_block_delta","index":0,"delta":{"type":"text_delta","text":"lo"}}

event: content_block_stop
data: {"type":"content_block_stop","index":0}

event: message_delta
data: {"type":"message_delta","delta":{"stop_reason":"end_turn"},"usage":{"output_tokens":57}}

event: message_stop
data: {"type":"message_stop"}

That is the Anthropic Messages stream (event names as documented; verify against the streaming docs). Note that the final token counts arrive at the end, in message_delta. OpenAI-compatible streams send data: {...} lines with choices[0].delta.content and finish with the literal line data: [DONE]; they report usage only if you ask (stream_options: {"include_usage": true}, verify).

Step by step.

  1. Client sends the normal request with "stream": true (or uses the SDK's streaming helper).
  2. Server starts generating, and after each small group of tokens writes one data: event and flushes.
  3. Client reads the response body incrementally, splits on blank lines, parses the JSON in data:, and appends the text delta to the UI.
  4. A terminal event (message_stop / [DONE]) says the stream ended normally. If the connection closes without it, the stream was cut and the answer is incomplete.

Time to first token (TTFT) versus total time. Streaming does not make the model faster. Total time is unchanged; TTFT is what improves, and TTFT is dominated by prefill, which prompt caching shortens. So caching and streaming multiply: a cache hit gives a quicker first token, streaming lets the user see it immediately.

Real life. A live sports commentary versus waiting for the match report in tomorrow's paper: same match, same total duration, but you follow it as it happens.

Common interview traps.

  • "Streaming reduces latency." It reduces perceived latency (time to first token), not total generation time.
  • Claiming SSE is bidirectional. It is server to client only; the request is a separate normal POST.
  • Forgetting that usage and stop reason arrive at the end of the stream, so cost accounting must wait for the last events.

notes.title: Streaming in code
notes.html:
Rule: prefer the SDK helper in Python (it handles parsing), and parse SSE yourself in Kotlin/Java only when you control the HTTP layer.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",   # verify model id
    max_tokens=500,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain SSE in two sentences."}],
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:       # yields each text delta as it arrives
        print(text, end="", flush=True)   # prints "Server-Sent..." gradually
    final = stream.get_final_message()    # complete message incl. usage
    print("\nusage:", final.usage)         # input / output / cache tokens for cost accounting
// Kotlin: server-side (or a JVM test) reading raw SSE with java.net.http, no SDK assumptions.
import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.HttpClient
import java.net.http.HttpRequest
import java.net.http.HttpResponse
import org.json.JSONObject

fun streamAnswer(prompt: String, onToken: (String) -> Unit) {
    val body = JSONObject()
        .put("model", "claude-sonnet-5-5").put("max_tokens", 500).put("stream", true)
        .put("messages", org.json.JSONArray().put(JSONObject().put("role", "user").put("content", prompt)))
    val req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"))
        .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
        .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01")
        .header("content-type", "application/json")
        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body.toString())).build()
    val res = HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofLines())
    res.body().use { lines ->
        lines.iterator().forEach { line ->
            if (!line.startsWith("data:")) return@forEach       // skip "event:" lines and blanks
            val ev = JSONObject(line.removePrefix("data:").trim())
            if (ev.optString("type") == "content_block_delta") {
                val d = ev.getJSONObject("delta")
                if (d.optString("type") == "text_delta") onToken(d.getString("text"))
            }
        }
    }
}
// On Android: the app talks to YOUR backend's SSE endpoint (OkHttp's okhttp-sse EventSource),
// collects tokens into a Kotlin Flow, and renders with Compose state. Keys stay on the server.
// Java 17 equivalent: same parsing, line by line.
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.util.function.Consumer;
import org.json.JSONObject;

public class Streamer {
    static void stream(String prompt, Consumer<String> onToken) throws Exception {
        String body = new JSONObject()
            .put("model", "claude-sonnet-5-5").put("max_tokens", 500).put("stream", true)
            .put("messages", new org.json.JSONArray()
                .put(new JSONObject().put("role", "user").put("content", prompt))).toString();
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"))
            .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
            .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01")
            .header("content-type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        HttpResponse<java.util.stream.Stream<String>> res =
            HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofLines());
        res.body().filter(l -> l.startsWith("data:")).forEach(l -> {
            JSONObject ev = new JSONObject(l.substring(5).trim());
            if ("content_block_delta".equals(ev.optString("type"))) {
                JSONObject d = ev.getJSONObject("delta");
                if ("text_delta".equals(d.optString("type"))) onToken.accept(d.getString("text"));
            }
        });
        // The official anthropic-java SDK also offers a streaming call; verify exact method names in its docs.
    }
}

Relaying to your own clients (Spring). A Spring MVC controller can return SseEmitter; WebFlux can return Flux<ServerSentEvent<String>>; Spring AI exposes ChatClient...stream() returning a Flux (verify current API). Your backend sits between the provider and the phone: it holds the key, applies quotas, and forwards deltas.

Real products. ChatGPT, Claude.ai and Gemini web apps all stream text; IDE assistants stream edits; voice products use WebSockets or WebRTC instead because they need two-way audio.

Real life. A tap that fills your glass while you watch, versus waiting for a full jug before anyone is allowed to drink.

Common interview traps.

  • Splitting the stream by TCP read size instead of by blank-line event boundaries; a JSON event can arrive in two chunks.
  • Updating the UI on every token without batching (Compose recomposes hundreds of times per second); coalesce to about 30 to 60 updates per second.
  • Reading usage from the first event only; the output token count is final only at message_delta.

notes.title: Streaming in production: proxies, cancellation and errors
notes.html:
Streaming works in a demo and fails in production for infrastructure reasons, almost never for model reasons.

  1. Buffering proxies. nginx, some CDNs and API gateways buffer responses. Symptom: the answer arrives all at once after a long wait. Fixes: proxy_buffering off; (nginx), send header X-Accel-Buffering: no, set Cache-Control: no-cache, disable gzip for the event stream or flush after each event (verify per gateway).
  2. Idle timeouts. A load balancer closing connections idle for 60 seconds kills long reasoning pauses. Send periodic SSE comment lines (: ping) as keep-alives. The provider itself may send ping events.
  3. Mid-stream errors. HTTP status 200 is already sent when generation starts, so a later failure arrives as an error event inside the stream (for example overloaded) rather than a 5xx. Your client must handle an error event and a connection that dies without a terminal event.
  4. Partial output policy. When the stream breaks at token 300 of 600, options are: show what you have and offer "continue"; retry from scratch (you pay twice for the prefix, minus cache hits); or prefill the assistant turn with the partial text and ask to continue (verify provider support). Decide per product.
  5. Cancellation and cost. If the user closes the tab, cancel the upstream request (close the HTTP connection, AbortController, coroutine cancellation). Otherwise you keep generating, and paying for, an answer nobody reads. Billing for a cancelled request typically covers tokens generated so far (verify).
  6. Backpressure. If the client reads slowly, the server must not buffer unbounded tokens per connection. Use bounded queues.
  7. Android specifics. OkHttp keeps streaming with a read timeout of 0 or a large one, otherwise it times out between sparse events. Mobile networks switch (Wi-Fi to LTE) and drop connections; resume by Last-Event-ID if your own server supports event ids, otherwise restart. Do not hold the stream across process death; persist the partial text.
  8. Structured output and tool calls. JSON arrives as fragments (input_json_delta for tool arguments); you must accumulate and parse only after the block stops. Rendering half-JSON is a classic bug.
  9. Moderation and post-processing. If you must scan the whole answer before showing it (compliance), streaming is incompatible, or you scan in sliding windows and accept a small risk.
 Phone ---SSE---> [your backend] ---SSE---> [provider]
   |                   |   ^  
   | close tab         |   | cancel upstream (otherwise tokens are billed)
   +------------------>+---+

Real life. Water through a long pipe with a narrow valve in the middle (a buffering proxy): the tap upstream runs freely but nothing comes out of the end until the valve opens.

Common interview traps.

  • "A 200 status means the stream succeeded." Errors can appear after the 200.
  • Not cancelling upstream on client disconnect.
  • Building a retry that resends the entire request after a cut stream without considering double billing.

notes.title: Quota management: provider usage limits
notes.html:
Plain words. Providers limit how much you can use, to keep the service fair and stable. Typical dimensions (names vary; verify in your provider's console):

  • RPM: requests per minute.
  • TPM (or ITPM and OTPM): tokens per minute, sometimes split into input and output.
  • Daily or monthly caps: token or dollar spend limits, tied to your usage tier (the more you have paid historically, the higher your limits).
  • Concurrency limits and, for batch APIs, a separate queue limit.
  • Limits are usually per organization and per model (or model family), not per API key.

What happens when you exceed them. HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a retry-after header (seconds). Provider-side overload is a different status (Anthropic uses 529 "overloaded"; OpenAI uses 503 or 429 variants; verify), and the right reaction to both is backoff, but 429 is your fault and 529/503 is theirs. Response headers like anthropic-ratelimit-requests-remaining and anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-reset tell you how much budget is left (verify exact header names).

How limiting is implemented: the token bucket. The bucket holds up to a capacity of "tokens" (here the word means rate-limit credits, not LLM tokens). It refills continuously at a fixed rate; each request takes credits; if the bucket is empty the request is rejected. This allows short bursts yet caps the average rate. Because of continuous refill, a limit of 60 RPM is effectively about 1 request per second, not "60 at the start of each minute", so bursts of 20 in one second can still produce 429.

Why tokens bind before requests: shown with numbers. Suppose your tier gives 50 RPM and 40,000 input TPM. Each request has 4,300 input tokens plus max_tokens = 1000. Some providers count an estimate of max output up front (verify), so charge 5,300 per request.

  • By requests: 50 per minute.
  • By tokens: 40,000 / 5,300 = 7.5 requests per minute.
  • The tokens limit binds, so only about 7 requests per minute are possible. Lowering max_tokens to a realistic 300 gives 40,000 / 4,600 = 8.7. Trimming the prompt matters far more than RPM tuning.
  • Interaction with caching: with Anthropic, cached read tokens generally do not count toward input TPM on current models (verify per model), which is a second reason to cache: caching raises your effective throughput under a fixed quota. With 4,000 of 4,300 tokens cached, a request counts roughly 300 input tokens: 40,000 / 1,300 = 30 requests per minute (still counting the 1,000 max output reservation if applicable).

Your own quotas. Provider limits protect the provider. You also need limits for your users and your wallet: per-user daily token budgets, per-tenant monthly spend caps, per-feature kill switches, alerts at 50/80/100% of budget, and a global circuit breaker. See 03_C1 for budget policy; here is the mechanism.

Strategies when you are near the limit.

  1. Client-side limiter (token bucket) in front of the SDK so you queue instead of bouncing off 429.
  2. Retry with exponential backoff plus jitter, honoring retry-after.
  3. Priority queues: interactive traffic first, batch/backfill traffic second (or move it to the batch API with its own limits).
  4. Multi-model or multi-provider fallback (Sonnet down to Haiku, or to another provider) with an eval-checked quality floor.
  5. Request a higher tier or provisioned throughput (committed capacity) for steady high volume.
  6. Reduce tokens: caching, shorter prompts, lower max_tokens.

Real life. A highway on-ramp meter light: it lets cars onto the road at a steady rate so the road does not jam, and a short burst of cars waits in a queue.

Common interview traps.

  • Only retrying on 429 and ignoring retry-after; hammering faster makes it worse.
  • Retrying without jitter; 1,000 clients retry at exactly the same second (thundering herd).
  • Setting max_tokens huge "just in case" and burning TPM budget on reservations.
  • Treating limits as per API key when they are per organization.

notes.title: Quota management in code
notes.html:
A small token-bucket limiter you place in front of calls, plus retry with backoff. Python first; the JVM versions show the same algorithm.

import random, threading, time
import anthropic

class TokenBucket:
    """Refills `rate` credits per second up to `capacity`. take(n) blocks until n credits exist."""
    def __init__(self, rate: float, capacity: float):
        self.rate, self.capacity = rate, capacity
        self.credits, self.last = capacity, time.monotonic()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def take(self, n: float):
        while True:
            with self.lock:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self.credits = min(self.capacity, self.credits + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
                self.last = now
                if self.credits >= n:
                    self.credits -= n
                    return
                wait = (n - self.credits) / self.rate   # seconds until enough credit
            time.sleep(wait)

# 40,000 tokens/minute -> 666.7 credits per second; allow bursts up to one minute of budget
tpm = TokenBucket(rate=40_000 / 60, capacity=40_000)
client = anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=0)  # we do our own retries (the SDK default is 2; verify)

def call(messages, est_tokens, attempts=5):
    for i in range(attempts):
        tpm.take(est_tokens)
        try:
            return client.messages.create(model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=300, messages=messages)
        except anthropic.RateLimitError as e:                # HTTP 429
            ra = e.response.headers.get("retry-after")
            delay = float(ra) if ra else min(30, 2 ** i)
            time.sleep(delay + random.uniform(0, 0.5 * delay))  # jitter
    raise RuntimeError("still rate limited after retries")
// Kotlin: same bucket with coroutines (kotlinx.coroutines).
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock

class TokenBucket(private val ratePerSec: Double, private val capacity: Double) {
    private var credits = capacity
    private var last = System.nanoTime()
    private val mutex = Mutex()

    suspend fun take(n: Double) {
        while (true) {
            val wait = mutex.withLock {
                val now = System.nanoTime()
                credits = minOf(capacity, credits + (now - last) / 1e9 * ratePerSec)
                last = now
                if (credits >= n) { credits -= n; return }
                (n - credits) / ratePerSec            // seconds to wait for enough credit
            }
            delay((wait * 1000).toLong())
        }
    }
}

suspend fun <T> withBackoff(attempts: Int = 5, block: suspend () -> T): T {
    for (i in 0 until attempts) {
        try { return block() }
        catch (e: RateLimited) {                      // your exception mapped from HTTP 429
            val base = e.retryAfterSeconds ?: minOf(30.0, Math.pow(2.0, i.toDouble()))
            delay(((base + Math.random() * 0.5 * base) * 1000).toLong())   // jitter
        }
    }
    error("still rate limited")
}
class RateLimited(val retryAfterSeconds: Double?) : Exception()
// Java: same algorithm with synchronized; per-user limiter would keep a Map<String, TokenBucket>.
public class TokenBucket {
    private final double ratePerSec, capacity;
    private double credits;
    private long last = System.nanoTime();

    public TokenBucket(double ratePerSec, double capacity) {
        this.ratePerSec = ratePerSec; this.capacity = capacity; this.credits = capacity;
    }

    public void take(double n) throws InterruptedException {
        while (true) {
            double wait;
            synchronized (this) {
                long now = System.nanoTime();
                credits = Math.min(capacity, credits + (now - last) / 1e9 * ratePerSec);
                last = now;
                if (credits >= n) { credits -= n; return; }
                wait = (n - credits) / ratePerSec;      // seconds until enough credit
            }
            Thread.sleep((long) (wait * 1000));
        }
    }

    // usage: new TokenBucket(40_000 / 60.0, 40_000).take(estimatedTokens);
}
// Spring users: Resilience4j RateLimiter / Bucket4j are production-grade alternatives.

Where to keep per-user budgets. In Redis with INCRBY on a key like budget:{user}:{yyyymmdd} plus an expiry, checked before the call and settled after the real usage is known (reserve the estimate, then adjust by actual minus estimate). In-process counters break when you run more than one instance.

Real products. API gateways such as LiteLLM, Portkey, Kong AI Gateway and OpenRouter provide per-key and per-team budgets, rate limits and fallbacks; many companies place such a gateway in front of every provider call (verify product features).

Real life. A prepaid mobile plan: a daily data allowance per person, a counter that is checked before you stream a video, and a top-up when it runs out.

Common interview traps.

  • Implementing the limiter per process while running 10 replicas; the real rate is 10x.
  • Estimating tokens by characters only; use the provider's token counting or a tokenizer for accuracy, and keep a safety margin.
  • Settling quota only on success; failed or cancelled requests may still consume tokens.

notes.title: Cost per request: the token-based formula
notes.html:
The formula. For one request:

cost = (fresh_input   x p_in)
     + (cache_write   x p_in x write_mult)       # e.g. 1.25 (verify)
     + (cache_read    x p_in x read_mult)        # e.g. 0.10 (verify)
     + (output_tokens x p_out)                   # includes hidden thinking tokens
   all prices are per token = (price per million) / 1,000,000

Where to read each number: the response usage block. Fresh input is input_tokens (for Anthropic this excludes cached tokens, which are reported separately; OpenAI's prompt_tokens includes the cached ones, so you subtract cached_tokens first. Check this per provider or your numbers will be wrong).

Worked example (illustrative prices, verify the current price page). Assume $3 per million input and $15 per million output. A support request has a 4,000-token static prefix (policy), 300 new input tokens, and 400 output tokens.

  • Without caching:
    • input: 4,300 x 3 / 1,000,000 = $0.0129
    • output: 400 x 15 / 1,000,000 = $0.0060
    • total: $0.0189
  • Cache read (hit):
    • cached input: 4,000 x 0.30 / 1,000,000 = $0.0012 (0.1 x $3 = $0.30 per million)
    • fresh input: 300 x 3 / 1,000,000 = $0.0009
    • output: $0.0060
    • total: $0.0081, which is 0.0081 / 0.0189 = 42.9% of the uncached price, so 57% cheaper.
  • Cache write (first call):
    • write: 4,000 x 3.75 / 1,000,000 = $0.0150 (1.25 x $3 = $3.75 per million)
    • fresh input $0.0009 + output $0.0060
    • total: $0.0219, 16% more than uncached, paid once per TTL window.

Monthly at 1,000,000 requests with a 95% hit ratio: 0.95 x 0.0081 + 0.05 x 0.0219 = 0.007695 + 0.001095 = $0.00879 per request, so $8,790 versus $18,900 uncached. That is a saving of $10,110 per month, from one change to prompt order.

Where else the money hides.

  • Output dominates short-prompt features. 100 input and 800 output tokens: input $0.0003, output $0.012. Cutting verbosity matters more than caching here.
  • Thinking tokens (extended reasoning) are billed as output even when not shown; a 5,000-token thinking budget adds 5,000 x 15 / 1,000,000 = $0.075 per request, which dwarfs the visible answer. Cap budgets and use reasoning only when needed.
  • Tool definitions and tool results are input tokens on every turn of an agent loop. A 20-turn agent whose context grows by 1,500 tokens per turn resends about 1,500 x (1 + 2 + ... + 20) = 1,500 x 210 = 315,000 input tokens in total, not 30,000. Caching the growing prefix is what makes agents affordable.
  • Images cost tokens by size; embeddings are separate and cheap per token; web search or other server tools have their own per-use fees (verify).
  • Retries and errors. A failed request that consumed tokens is still billed. Counting only successful responses under-reports spend by the retry rate.
  • Batch discount. Asynchronous batch APIs commonly give about 50% off in exchange for up to a 24-hour turnaround (verify), and it can stack with caching.
  • Model tier. The same call on a small model can cost an order of magnitude less; routing easy requests to it is the biggest lever (see 03_C1).

Cost per outcome, not per request. The number a business cares about is cost per resolved ticket, per summarised document, per accepted code suggestion. A cheap model with a 60% success rate and a human fallback may cost more per resolved ticket than a stronger model at 90%.

Real life. A taxi fare: a base charge (fresh input), a cheaper rate for the stretch you have driven before (cache read), a higher rate per kilometre of the trip you actually add (output), and a surcharge for first-time route setup (cache write).

Common interview traps.

  • Using prompt_tokens and cached_tokens as if they were disjoint; on OpenAI-style usage one is a subset of the other.
  • Forgetting hidden reasoning tokens and the write premium.
  • Quoting a monthly cost from the average request when the distribution has a heavy tail (a few huge prompts); compute percentiles, not just the mean.

notes.title: Cost per request in code
notes.html:
Compute it from the usage block, log it with business tags, and aggregate. Keep prices in config with a date, because they change.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Price:                  # USD per million tokens (illustrative; load from config, verify)
    inp: float
    out: float
    write_mult: float = 1.25
    read_mult: float = 0.10

PRICES = {"claude-sonnet-5-5": Price(3.0, 15.0)}

def cost_usd(model: str, usage) -> float:
    p = PRICES[model]
    m = 1_000_000
    return (usage.input_tokens * p.inp
            + usage.cache_creation_input_tokens * p.inp * p.write_mult
            + usage.cache_read_input_tokens * p.inp * p.read_mult
            + usage.output_tokens * p.out) / m

# self-check with the worked example: 300 fresh, 4000 cache read, 400 out -> 0.0081
class U: input_tokens=300; cache_creation_input_tokens=0; cache_read_input_tokens=4000; output_tokens=400
assert abs(cost_usd("claude-sonnet-5-5", U) - 0.0081) < 1e-9
data class Price(val inp: Double, val out: Double, val writeMult: Double = 1.25, val readMult: Double = 0.10)
data class Usage(val input: Long, val cacheWrite: Long, val cacheRead: Long, val output: Long)

val prices = mapOf("claude-sonnet-5-5" to Price(3.0, 15.0)) // USD per million; verify and load from config

fun costUsd(model: String, u: Usage): Double {
    val p = prices.getValue(model)
    return (u.input * p.inp
        + u.cacheWrite * p.inp * p.writeMult
        + u.cacheRead * p.inp * p.readMult
        + u.output * p.out) / 1_000_000.0
}

fun main() {
    println(costUsd("claude-sonnet-5-5", Usage(300, 0, 4000, 400))) // prints about 0.0081
}
import java.util.Map;

public class Cost {
    record Price(double in, double out, double writeMult, double readMult) {}
    record Usage(long input, long cacheWrite, long cacheRead, long output) {}

    // USD per million tokens; illustrative, verify and load from config
    static final Map<String, Price> PRICES =
        Map.of("claude-sonnet-5-5", new Price(3.0, 15.0, 1.25, 0.10));

    static double costUsd(String model, Usage u) {
        Price p = PRICES.get(model);
        return (u.input() * p.in()
              + u.cacheWrite() * p.in() * p.writeMult()
              + u.cacheRead() * p.in() * p.readMult()
              + u.output() * p.out()) / 1_000_000.0;
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(costUsd("claude-sonnet-5-5", new Usage(300, 0, 4000, 400))); // about 0.0081
    }
}

Operational pattern. After every call (including streamed calls, after the final usage event), emit one structured log line or metric: feature, tenant, model, prompt_version, fresh, cache_write, cache_read, output, latency_ttft_ms, latency_total_ms, cost_usd, status. Dashboards then show cost by feature, cache hit ratio, p95 TTFT and 429 rate on one screen. Alerts: cost per request p95 up 30% after a deploy, hit ratio below a floor, spend crossing a budget line. Tools such as Langfuse, Helicone, LangSmith, and the provider consoles do this aggregation (verify features). On Android, never compute billing on device; the backend knows the real usage.

Real life. A shop's till receipt that lists every item, then the daily sheet that adds the receipts up so the owner can see which product earns or loses money.

Common interview traps.

  • Hard-coding prices in code; prices and model names change, so use versioned config.
  • Using floating point for money in billing records; for invoices use integer micro-dollars or BigDecimal. Floats are fine for estimates and dashboards.
  • Estimating cost before the call from max_tokens and reporting it as actual cost.

notes.title: Putting the four together: a design walk-through
notes.html:
Scenario: a document-QA chat in an Android app. Each user uploads a 20,000-token contract and asks 8 questions in a session. Model price as above ($3 / $15 per million, illustrative).

  1. Prompt layout. [system rules][contract 20,000 tok]* [history] [question]. Breakpoint after the contract. Also advance a breakpoint on the history for turns beyond the first.
  2. Cost without caching. Each question resends 20,000 + about 500 tokens: 8 x 20,500 x 3 / 1,000,000 = $0.492 input, plus output 8 x 400 x 15 / 1,000,000 = $0.048. Total about $0.540 per session.
  3. Cost with caching. Write once: 20,000 x 3.75 / 1,000,000 = $0.075. Seven reads: 7 x 20,000 x 0.30 / 1,000,000 = $0.042. Fresh tokens: 8 x 500 x 3 / 1,000,000 = $0.012. Output $0.048. Total about $0.177, a 67% reduction (0.177 / 0.540 = 0.328).
  4. Latency. Question 1 pays the full prefill of 20,000 tokens (a couple of seconds on a large model; verify). Questions 2 to 8 skip it, and streaming shows the first words in well under a second.
  5. Quota. Uncached, one question counts about 20,500 input tokens against TPM; at a 400,000 TPM tier that is under 20 questions per minute across ALL users. With cached reads not counting (verify), the same tier supports several times more. Add a per-user bucket so one user cannot starve others, and a queue with retry-after handling for the rest.
  6. Streaming path. Phone connects by SSE (or OkHttp EventSource) to your backend; backend streams from the provider; client cancel closes the upstream call; the final usage event triggers the cost log and the quota settlement.
  7. Safety nets. Per-user daily token budget in Redis; global kill switch if hourly spend passes a threshold; alert on hit ratio below 80%; fallback to the smaller model on repeated 529 with a flag in the UI.
 Android app --SSE--> Backend ---------------------------> Provider
                      | per-user token bucket (Redis)       | cache hit: skip 20k prefill
                      | prefix: static first, breakpoint    | stream deltas
                      | cancel upstream on disconnect       | final usage: read/write/fresh/out
                      +--> cost log + dashboards <----------+

Real products doing this. Chat-with-your-PDF tools, enterprise knowledge assistants, and coding assistants all use this same four-part pattern: cache the big context, stream the answer, rate-limit per user and per tenant, and log cost per request.

Real life. Running a food truck: prep the base sauce once (cache), serve plates as they are ready (stream), cap the queue length so the kitchen does not collapse (quota), and tally the till each evening (cost).

Common interview traps.

  • Designing the prompt with the user question first and the document last; nothing gets cached.
  • Claiming a saving percentage without showing the token maths; interviewers expect the arithmetic.
  • Ignoring the first-request latency: a cache write is not faster than normal.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Prompt caching reuses the processed exact prefix of your prompt. Order: static content first (tools, system, documents), dynamic content last, a breakpoint at the end of the static part. Reads cost a small fraction (about 0.1x), writes a premium (about 1.25x for the short TTL), so it pays from the second request inside the TTL. It does not cache answers. Verify hit rates through the usage fields; zero reads means a changing prefix, a too-short prefix, or an expired TTL.
  • SSE is a one-way server-to-client stream of event: / data: blocks separated by blank lines over a normal HTTP response. It improves time to first token, not total time. In production the problems are buffering proxies, idle timeouts, errors after the 200, cancelling upstream, and accumulating partial JSON. Final token counts arrive at the end.
  • Quotas come as RPM, TPM, daily/monthly caps and concurrency, per organization and model. A 429 carries retry-after; use a client-side token bucket, exponential backoff with jitter, priority queues, fallbacks and higher tiers. Tokens usually bind before requests, and caching raises effective throughput. Keep your own per-user budgets in shared storage such as Redis.
  • Cost per request is fresh x p_in + write x 1.25 p_in + read x 0.1 p_in + output x p_out, computed from the response usage, with prices from versioned config. Output, thinking tokens, agent-loop resending and retries are the usual surprises. Measure cost per outcome, log every call, and alert on regressions.
  • All prices, multipliers, minimum lengths, TTLs, limit numbers and header names above are illustrative or fast-moving: verify against the provider docs before relying on them.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up the layers: provider prompt cache, your response cache, and semantic cache.
  • Quoting savings or limits without the arithmetic or the "verify current docs" caveat.
  • Treating streaming, caching, quotas and cost as separate topics when a single prefix change or a missing cancel can break all four.
